newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr topples, rally built on sand.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr topples, rally built on sand.

text.p: The Australian dollar sagged back to support Wednesday as a painstakingly constructed rally above US$0.7950 proved to be build on sand.

Four days of consolidation had seen the currency refreshed enough to clear that important chart barrier offshore Tuesday, reaching as high as US$0.7970. But the gains unravelled when an alarmingly strong Japanese trade report sent US$/yen sliding.

The selling spilled over into the crosses, swept the dollar back under US$.7950 and squeezed speculators out of their long positions. It also undermined its technical foundations leaving many looking for a test of US$0.7910 on route to US$0.7850.
"The Aussie's struggling," said David de Garis, a Treasury economist at ANZ Bank. "Our view is for a further softening with the AUD down in the 78's over the next month."
By 4.30 pm (0530 GMT) the dollar was looking a little worse for wear at US$0.7925/30 after toppling from an early US$0.7960/65, and was even down on Tuesday's late US$0.7935/40.
The rot set in when Japan reported the first rise in its overall trade surplus in two years and markets, fearing a fresh outbreak of trade hostilities, dumped US$/yen.
The local currency followed to finish at 90.02/12 yen from an early 90.65/75 and 90.24/34 late here Tuesday.
In trade weighted terms it was back where it began at 58.9.
Dealers emphasised that much depended on how US$/yen fared from here and noted it had steadied for the moment at 113.60 yen support having dipped as far as 113.35 from an early 113.85/90.
The rise in Japan's November trade surplus was only a slight 0.2 percent to 675.19 billion yen, but that was big shock given analysts had been tipping a 28 percent fall.

The surprise came in exports which rose 10 percent thanks chiefly to a 27.7 percent rise in car exports. That in turn was considered largely a function of the weaker yen which reduced the price of Japanese cars sold abroad.

Analysts noted U.S. automobile manufacturers had been saying for months that the yen was too low for them to compete and after these figures, they were worried their complaints would carry more weight in Washington.
If trade tensions did increase, then both dollars were likely to suffer they said.

And any threat of slippage against the yen was particularly dangerous for the A$ since Japanese investors had bankrolled much of its hefty gains this year. They were unlikely to take kindly to increased currency risk at a time when the A$'s yield premium had just been slashed by an official rate cut.
Analysts also reckoned the easing cycle might not be over.
"What we're going to see is pretty good inflation numbers... which will raise the prospect the Reserve Bank might cut rates again," said de Garis at ANZ.
"The market has not fully priced that in as yet so it could weigh on the AUD for the next few months," he said.
The Japanese trade figures rather overshadowed domestic news on merchandise imports for November.
Imports rose 1.2 percent, before rounding, after a 1.3 percent gain in October and almost exactly matched market forecasts of a 1.0 percent increase.
The breakdown showed consumption goods imports up 1.9 percent, capital goods rose 6.2 percent and intermediate goods imports eased 1.3 percent.
In this case the gains were viewed as positive for the dollar since they suggested that consumer demand and business investment were picking up once again after some months of softness.

Also out was the Westpac leading index of economic activity for October which rose a relatively healthy 1.7 percent, reinforcing market expectations for a steady pick up in growth next year. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
